./.title: Introduction
./.body:
The Expanding Universe & The Big Bang Model
Second Edition, 2026
Author: Alex C Punnen
Based on the author's B.Sc Physics Project Report of 1998

This is a revised edition of a project report written in 1998. The first edition is kept unchanged as a record of what was written then; this edition uses it as a base and adds:

New diagrams. Every figure has been redrawn from physics or from published, cited measurements. The scanned textbook figures of the original have been replaced. The figures are produced by a script (scripts/make_figures.py), so anyone can regenerate or check them.
Corrections. Errors in the original, from a wrong proportionality in the Cepheid law to a misdated quotation, are fixed. Each one is listed in Changes from the First Edition.
Fuller explanations where the original skipped a step, for example why the Big Bang produces about 25% helium.
A new Part III, describing what has been learned since 1998: the year the Universe was found to be accelerating.

Contents
Part I: The Expanding Universe

Methods in Observational Astronomy
Estimating the Distance Scale of the Universe
Expansion of the Universe

Part II: The Big Bang Model of the Origin of the Universe

Distribution of Radio Galaxies and Quasars
Olbers' Paradox and Its Resolution
The Prediction of Cosmic Background Radiation
The Discovery of Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation
The Hot Big Bang
Big Bang Nucleosynthesis
Conclusion

Part III: Since 1998

The Universe Since 1998

Back Matter

Changes from the First Edition
References and Further Reading


Numbers quoted for the present-day Universe use the Planck 2018 cosmological parameters (H₀ = 67.4 km/s/Mpc, 31.5% matter, 68.5% dark energy, age 13.8 billion years) unless stated otherwise.

preface.html.title: Preface
preface.html.body:
Preface
Preface to the Second Edition
In 1998 I wrote a short report, as a physics undergraduate, on two discoveries that seemed to me the greatest of the century: that the Universe is expanding, and that it began in a hot, dense state. That same year, two teams of astronomers announced that the expansion is not slowing down, as everyone had expected, but speeding up. The report does not mention it.
This edition keeps the shape and the argument of the original: the climb up the distance ladder, Hubble's law, and the three pillars of evidence for the Big Bang. It corrects what was wrong, explains what was skipped, replaces the borrowed textbook figures with new diagrams, and ends with a new chapter on what nearly three decades of observation have added. The first edition remains available, unchanged, alongside this one.
Preface to the First Edition (1998)
Amidst the boundless, infinite Universe, humanity and its world are but a mere speck of physical insignificance. But our imagination is infinite and boundless; and those greats of our race, who have put their imagination, intuition and deduction to harmonious use, have come up with amazing facts of our Universe and great theories to account for the observations.
In the following account two of the greatest scientific discoveries of our time, that is, the discovery of the Expanding Universe and the Big Bang theory of the origin of the Universe, are presented with an account of the observational and theoretical methods employed in the discovery.

chapters/ch01-methods-observational-astr.title: Chapter 1: Methods in Observational Astronomy
chapters/ch01-methods-observational-astr.body:
Chapter 1: Methods in Observational Astronomy
Almost everything we know about the Universe beyond the Solar System has arrived as light. Astronomy is therefore the art of collecting as much of that light as possible, and of squeezing every bit of information out of it: how bright the source is, what colour it is, and which wavelengths are missing from its spectrum.
1.1 Astronomical Telescopes
Telescopes can use either refraction (lenses) or reflection (mirrors) to gather light over a large collecting surface and bring it to a focus on a much smaller area. This ability to gather light, and not magnification, is the primary purpose of an astronomical telescope.
Two numbers describe what a telescope can do, and both depend on the diameter D of its main lens or mirror:

Light-gathering power ∝ D² (the collecting area)
Smallest resolvable angle θ ≈ 1.22 λ / D (the diffraction limit)

Doubling the aperture collects four times the light, so stars four times fainter become visible.

Figure 1.1. Light-gathering power grows as the square of the aperture. The 40-inch (1.02 m) Yerkes refractor of 1897 is still the largest lens telescope ever used for astronomy; every larger telescope is a reflector.
Why reflectors won
Refracting telescopes have serious drawbacks. A lens bends different colours by different amounts (chromatic aberration), so the images have coloured fringes. A lens can be supported only at its edge, so a large lens sags under its own weight. And light must pass through the glass, which absorbs some of it, particularly in the ultraviolet. The 1-metre Yerkes lens reached the practical limit.
A mirror has none of these problems: reflection treats all colours alike, and a mirror can be supported across its entire back. For these reasons all large modern telescopes are reflectors.
Reflecting telescopes
The main element of a reflecting telescope is a concave mirror with a paraboloidal surface, which brings all light from a distant point source to a single focus. Because secondary mirrors can easily redirect the beam, several different focal arrangements are possible, each with a different focal ratio. This lets a single telescope serve several different purposes efficiently.

Figure 1.2. Focal arrangements of a reflecting telescope. (a) Prime focus: the detector sits in the beam, in front of the primary mirror; this gives the widest field. (b) Newtonian: a flat diagonal mirror sends the beam out of the side of the tube. (c) Cassegrain: a convex secondary mirror sends the beam back through a hole in the primary; this gives a long focal length in a short tube. (d) Coudé: extra flat mirrors send the beam to a fixed room, where heavy spectrographs can be mounted that would be impossible to swing around with the telescope.
1.2 Detectors: from the Eye to the CCD
Gathering light is only half the job; it must also be recorded.

Photographic plates (from the 1880s) allowed exposures of many hours, accumulating light that the eye could never see. Hubble's discoveries in Chapter 3 were all made on photographic plates. But a plate records only about 1–2% of the photons that fall on it.
Charge-coupled devices (CCDs), adopted by astronomers from the late 1970s, record up to about 90% of the photons and give a direct digital measurement of brightness. A modest telescope with a CCD can outperform a giant one using plates.

1.3 Spectroscopy
A spectrograph spreads the light from a star or galaxy into its component wavelengths. The resulting spectrum is the single most informative thing an astronomer can measure:

its overall shape gives the temperature of the source (Chapter 2);
dark absorption lines at characteristic wavelengths reveal the chemical composition;
a shift of those lines from their laboratory wavelengths gives the velocity of the source along the line of sight, through the Doppler effect. This is how the expansion of the Universe was discovered (Chapter 3).

1.4 Beyond Visible Light
The atmosphere is transparent to visible light and to radio waves, but blocks most other wavelengths. Radio telescopes, developed after the Second World War, opened the second window. They found the radio galaxies and quasars of Chapter 4 and the cosmic microwave background of Chapter 7. Space telescopes avoid the atmosphere entirely. The Hubble Space Telescope (launched 1990) and the James Webb Space Telescope (launched 2021) have produced many of the results described in Chapter 11.

chapters/ch02-distance-scale.html.title: Chapter 2: Estimating the Distance Scale of the Universe
chapters/ch02-distance-scale.html.body:
Chapter 2: Estimating the Distance Scale of the Universe
Measuring how far away things are is the hardest basic problem in astronomy. A star looks like a point of light whether it is near and faint or far and luminous. No single method works at every distance. Instead, astronomers have built a distance ladder: each method is calibrated using the one below it and then reaches further out.

Figure 2.1. The rungs of the distance ladder and the range over which each works. Overlaps between rungs are what allow each one to be calibrated from the one above it in this chart.
A useful bookkeeping quantity throughout this chapter is the distance modulus. If m is a star's apparent magnitude (how bright it looks) and M its absolute magnitude (how bright it would look from 10 parsecs), then

m − M = 5 log₁₀ (d / 10 pc)

Magnitudes run backwards, so smaller numbers mean brighter. A difference of 5 magnitudes is a factor of 100 in brightness. Knowing m − M is the same as knowing the distance.
2.1 Trigonometric Parallax
This is the oldest and most direct method, and the foundation of the whole ladder. As the Earth moves around the Sun, a nearby star appears to shift back and forth against much more distant background stars. Six months apart, the Earth is at opposite ends of a baseline 2 AU long.

Figure 2.2. Trigonometric parallax. The parallax angle p is half the total shift seen over six months. The star appears projected to the right of its mean position when seen from one side of the orbit, and to the left from the other.
Treating the background stars as infinitely far away, simple geometry gives the distance:

d = 1 AU / p (p in radians)

Astronomers define the parsec (pc) as the distance at which p = 1 arcsecond, so that

d (pc) = 1 / p (arcsec),   1 pc = 3.26 light-years = 206 265 AU.

The angles are tiny. Even the nearest star, Proxima Centauri, has p = 0.77″, the size of a coin seen from 5 km away. From the ground, through a shimmering atmosphere, parallaxes could be measured reliably only for stars within about 100 pc (around 300 light-years). Measurements from space changed that. The Hipparcos satellite (1989–93) reached about 1 milliarcsecond. The Gaia satellite (launched 2013) measures parallaxes for more than a billion stars, some to a few hundredths of a milliarcsecond, and gives accurate distances to thousands of parsecs.
2.2 The Hertzsprung–Russell Diagram
Many properties of a star, even its distance, can be found from its position in the Hertzsprung–Russell (H-R) diagram, a plot of luminosity L against surface temperature Tₑ. First, how are L and Tₑ measured?
Luminosity
Two measurements are needed:

(a) the apparent brightness f, the energy received from the star per unit time per unit area at the Earth; and
(b) the distance d, from parallax or (for clusters) the moving-cluster method.

The star's energy spreads over a sphere of area 4πd², so

L = 4π d² f

Effective temperature
There are two independent methods.
(i) Colour photometry (UBV). A hot body emits a larger fraction of its energy at short wavelengths than a cool one does. Measuring the brightness through standard ultraviolet (U), blue (B) and visual (V) filters therefore gives the temperature. In practice the ratio is expressed as a colour index, B − V, the difference between the magnitudes in the two filters. Hot stars have B − V near zero or negative; cool red stars have B − V of 1.5 or more.

Figure 2.3. Blackbody spectra at three temperatures, scaled to match in the V band. The hot star is much brighter in B and U than in V; the cool star is fainter. The ratio, i.e. the colour, measures the temperature without needing the distance.
(ii) Spectral classification. For a given chemical composition, the pattern of absorption lines formed in a star's atmosphere depends mainly on its temperature. Hydrogen lines are strongest near 10 000 K. Ionised helium lines appear only in the hottest stars, and molecular bands only in the coolest. Stars are sorted into the spectral sequence O B A F G K M, from hottest (about 40 000 K) to coolest (about 3 000 K), and the spectral type gives the temperature.
The main sequence
When L is plotted against Tₑ for stars of known distance, the points are not scattered at random. About 90% of stars lie on a narrow diagonal band, the main sequence. These are stars steadily fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores. A star's position along the main sequence is set by its mass: massive stars are hot and extremely luminous, and low-mass stars are cool and faint.

Figure 2.4. A schematic H-R diagram. Temperature increases to the left, by convention. The main sequence runs from hot, luminous, massive stars (upper left) to cool, faint, low-mass stars (lower right); masses are marked along it. Giants, supergiants and white dwarfs are stars in later stages of their lives.
2.3 Star Clusters and Main-Sequence Fitting
A star cluster is a group of stars born together from the same cloud of gas. Its stars have the same age and composition and, because a cluster's angular size is small, all of them are at essentially the same distance from us. Two kinds are found in our Galaxy: loose, young open clusters, and dense, ancient globular clusters.
Because every star in a cluster is at the same distance, plotting their apparent magnitudes against colour gives the shape of the H-R diagram exactly; only the vertical scale is unknown. Robert Trumpler realised in the 1920s that this allows clusters to be compared. If the main sequence of one cluster lies 5 magnitudes lower than that of another, its stars look 100 times fainter, so it is 10 times further away.
This is main-sequence fitting. Theory and observation show that all unevolved stars of the same composition lie on the same line in the colour–magnitude diagram, the zero-age main sequence (ZAMS). For a cluster whose distance is known (the Hyades), the main sequence can be drawn in absolute magnitude M_V. For any other cluster we measure only apparent magnitude m_V. Sliding its main sequence vertically until it lies on top of the Hyades' gives the distance modulus directly.

Figure 2.5. Main-sequence fitting. At any given colour, the vertical shift between the distant cluster's main sequence (apparent magnitudes) and the calibrating main sequence (absolute magnitudes) is the distance modulus m − M. Here it is 9 magnitudes, corresponding to about 630 pc.
The whole method therefore rests on knowing the distance to one cluster accurately. That cluster is the Hyades.
2.4 The Distance to the Hyades: the Moving-Cluster Method
The Hyades, in Taurus, is the nearest well-populated open cluster. Its stars all move through space together, along parallel paths with the same velocity V. Parallel lines viewed in perspective appear to meet at a point, as railway tracks do at the horizon. The proper motions of the Hyades stars, traced across the sky, all point towards a single convergent point, which shows the direction of V.

Figure 2.6. The moving-cluster method. The cluster's common space velocity V points towards the convergent point, at angle θ from our line of sight to the cluster. The Doppler shift gives the component along the line of sight, v_r = V cos θ. The proper motion μ gives the angular rate of the sideways component, v_t = V sin θ = 4.74 μ d.
Measuring θ from the convergent point and v_r from the Doppler shift gives the true sideways speed v_t = v_r tan θ in km/s. The same sideways motion is seen on the sky as an angular speed μ. Comparing the two gives the distance:

d (pc) = v_r tan θ / (4.74 μ)   (v_r in km/s, μ in arcsec per year)

An equivalent way to picture this: the Hyades is moving away from us, so over the decades it appears to shrink slightly, and the rate of shrinking, combined with its speed of recession, also gives its distance.
The method gave a Hyades distance of about 46 pc. Hipparcos and Gaia have since measured the parallaxes of individual Hyades stars directly, giving 47 pc, in excellent agreement.
2.5 Cepheid Variables as Distance Indicators
Main-sequence fitting fails for clusters so distant that their ordinary main-sequence stars are too faint to measure. To go further, a much more luminous kind of star is needed whose luminosity can be found without knowing its distance. The Cepheid variables are such stars.
Cepheids are yellow supergiants that pulsate: they swell and shrink regularly, and their brightness rises and falls with periods of 1 to 100 days. The prototype, δ Cephei, can be seen with the naked eye.

Figure 2.7. The light curve of δ Cephei. The star brightens quickly and fades slowly, repeating every 5.37 days.
In 1912 Henrietta Swan Leavitt, studying Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud (all of which are at essentially the same distance from us), discovered that the longer the period, the more luminous the star. The relation is not a simple proportion. Luminosity grows roughly as a power of the period, so on logarithmic axes it is a straight line:

log L = a log P + b, or equivalently M_V = α (log P − 1) + β

A modern calibration, using Hubble Space Telescope parallaxes of nearby Cepheids, is

M_V = −2.43 (log₁₀ P − 1) − 4.05   (P in days)

so a 10-day Cepheid has M_V ≈ −4.05, about 3 500 times as luminous as the Sun, and each tenfold increase in period makes the star about 9 times more luminous.

Figure 2.8. The period–luminosity (Leavitt) law. Plotted on a logarithmic period axis, absolute magnitude falls along a straight line. Measure a Cepheid's period, read off its absolute magnitude, compare with its apparent magnitude, and the distance follows.
The procedure is:

Calibrate the zero-point β using Cepheids whose distances are known independently: a few lie in open clusters whose distances come from main-sequence fitting, and today many have Gaia parallaxes.
Measure the period of a distant Cepheid from its light curve and read off M_V.
Measure its apparent magnitude m_V. Then m_V − M_V gives the distance.

Because Cepheids are thousands of times more luminous than the Sun, they can be seen in other galaxies. The period–luminosity relation was the means by which astronomers extended the distance scale beyond our own Galaxy. This is the subject of the next chapter.

A historical pitfall. In 1952 Walter Baade showed that there are two distinct kinds of Cepheid, differing by a factor of about 4 in luminosity at the same period. They had been mixed up in the calibration. Correcting the mistake doubled all extragalactic distances at a stroke. It was the largest single revision ever made to the size of the Universe.

chapters/ch03-expansion-of-universe.html.title: Chapter 3: Expansion of the Universe
chapters/ch03-expansion-of-universe.html.body:
Chapter 3: Expansion of the Universe
At the start of the 1920s it was still an open question whether the faint spiral "nebulae" were clouds of gas inside our own Milky Way or separate galaxies far beyond it. The question was settled with the tools of Chapter 2.
In 1923–24, using the 100-inch (2.5 m) Hooker telescope at Mount Wilson, Edwin Hubble found Cepheid variables in the Andromeda nebula, M31, and in other spirals. Their periods and faintness placed them far outside the Milky Way: the spirals were galaxies in their own right. (Hubble's distances were later revised upwards by Baade's correction; Andromeda is about 770 kpc, 2.5 million light-years, away.)
3.1 Redshifts
Since 1912, Vesto Slipher at Lowell Observatory had been measuring the spectra of spiral nebulae. He found that the absorption lines of most of them were shifted towards the red end of the spectrum, often by large amounts. The shift is described by the redshift

z = (λ_observed − λ_emitted) / λ_emitted

Every line in the spectrum is shifted by the same factor (1 + z). This is how a redshift is distinguished from a change in the lines themselves. For small redshifts, the Doppler formula gives the velocity of recession: v ≈ cz.

Figure 3.1. The same set of absorption lines, at rest in the laboratory (top) and in the spectrum of a galaxy with z = 0.04 (bottom). Each line moves to a longer wavelength by 4%. The pattern is unchanged, so the lines can still be identified.
3.2 Hubble's Law
In 1929 Hubble combined Slipher's velocities, and new ones measured by Milton Humason, with his own Cepheid-based distances for 24 galaxies. Apart from a few nearby galaxies, all were receding. When velocity was plotted against distance, the points scattered about a straight line: the recession velocity is proportional to the distance.

v = H₀ d

This is Hubble's law, and the constant of proportionality H₀ is the Hubble constant. (Georges Lemaître had derived the same relation from Einstein's equations and estimated its slope from published data in 1927, two years before Hubble. In 2018 the International Astronomical Union recommended the name Hubble–Lemaître law.)

Figure 3.2. Hubble's law at the scale of the original 1929 data (left; galaxies within 2 Mpc, velocities up to about 1 000 km/s) and at the scale of modern data (right; hundreds of Mpc). The points are illustrative. Hubble's slope of about 500 km/s/Mpc was far too steep, because his distances were underestimated, but the straight-line relation survived every later test.
Hubble's own value of H₀ was about 500 km/s/Mpc. The distances were too small, partly because of the Cepheid confusion described at the end of Chapter 2 and partly because some of the "brightest stars" he used in distant galaxies were really glowing clouds of ionised gas, far more luminous than any star. The modern value is close to 70 km/s/Mpc. A galaxy 100 Mpc away recedes at about 7 000 km/s. (The small disagreement between methods about the exact value is one of the open problems of Chapter 11.)
3.3 What Hubble's Law Means
Hubble himself was cautious about drawing a grand conclusion from so few galaxies. The redshifts might not be Doppler shifts at all. Within two years, however, Humason had measured galaxies in distant clusters receding at nearly 20 000 km/s, and the straight line still held. The law was soon widely accepted.
A linear velocity–distance law has a remarkable property. It describes a Universe in which every distance is growing by the same factor, and it looks the same from every galaxy. Figure 3.3 shows why.

Figure 3.3. Uniform expansion. Between the two panels every distance has grown by 50%. Measured from our galaxy, each other galaxy has moved by an amount proportional to its distance, which is Hubble's law. Choose any other galaxy as the centre and the same is true. Hubble's law does not put us at the centre of anything.
The right picture is not of galaxies flying apart through a pre-existing space, but of space itself stretching, carrying the galaxies with it. It is described by a single scale factor, a(t), which multiplies all cosmic distances. In this picture the cosmological redshift is not really a Doppler shift. Light waves are stretched along with the space they travel through, so

1 + z = a(today) / a(when the light was emitted)

A galaxy at redshift z = 1 is seen as it was when the Universe was half its present size.
3.4 The Age of the Universe
If the galaxies are moving apart now, they were closer together in the past. Run the expansion backwards and, at some finite time ago, all the matter in the observable Universe was packed extremely closely together. This is the seed of the Big Bang theory: the Universe had a beginning in time.
A first estimate of when is simple. If each galaxy has moved at constant speed v, then the time it took to reach its present distance d is

t₀ = d / v = d / (H₀ d) = 1 / H₀

The same for every galaxy. The quantity 1/H₀ is called the Hubble time. Converting units (1 Mpc = 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km):

1/H₀ = 977.8 / H₀ billion years (H₀ in km/s/Mpc)

so H₀ = 70 gives 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. (Hubble's original value of 500 gave under 2 billion years, younger than the Earth. That embarrassment helped motivate the rival steady-state theory discussed in Part II.)
The true age differs from 1/H₀ because the expansion rate has not been constant. Gravity slows the expansion; dark energy (Chapter 11) speeds it up.

Figure 3.4. How the size of the Universe changes with time in three models, all with the same expansion rate today. An empty universe coasts and its age is exactly 1/H₀. A universe containing only matter decelerates and is younger, ⅔ × 1/H₀. The observed Universe (ΛCDM) decelerated at first and has been accelerating for the last few billion years; by coincidence its age, 13.8 billion years, is close to 1/H₀.
3.5 Mapping the Large-Scale Structure of the Universe
Because velocity and distance are proportional, and redshifts are easy to measure, the redshift itself is used as the distance indicator for remote galaxies. Measuring redshifts for many galaxies across a patch of sky gives a three-dimensional map of the Universe.
In the 1980s the Harvard–Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (CfA) redshift survey produced the first such map, a thin slice of sky containing about 1 000 galaxies. It showed that galaxies are not spread evenly. They lie along filaments and on the walls of enormous voids some 50 Mpc across. In the centre of the CfA slice the Coma cluster forms the body of a famous "stick man".
Spectrographs fed by optical fibres, each fibre placed on one galaxy, now measure hundreds or thousands of redshifts in a single exposure. The 2dF Galaxy Redshift Survey (about 220 000 galaxies, completed 2003), the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (millions of galaxies) and the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI, 5 000 fibres, operating since 2021) have mapped this cosmic web to distances of billions of light-years. On the very largest scales, above a few hundred megaparsecs, the Universe becomes smooth, as the Big Bang model assumes.

chapters/ch04-radio-galaxies-quasars.htm.title: Chapter 4: Distribution of Radio Galaxies and Quasars
chapters/ch04-radio-galaxies-quasars.htm.body:
Chapter 4: Distribution of Radio Galaxies and Quasars
Two theories of an expanding Universe
By the late 1940s there were two ways to reconcile the expansion of Chapter 3 with the rest of physics.

The Big Bang theory: the Universe began in a hot, dense state a finite time ago and has been expanding, cooling and changing ever since. The Universe of the past was different from the Universe of today.
The steady-state theory, proposed in 1948 by Hermann Bondi, Thomas Gold and Fred Hoyle. It rests on the perfect cosmological principle: the Universe looks the same not only from every place but at every time. As galaxies move apart, new matter is continuously created to form new galaxies in the gaps, keeping the average density constant. Such a Universe has no beginning and does not evolve.

(The name "Big Bang" was coined by Hoyle in a 1949 BBC radio broadcast.)
The two theories make one sharply different prediction. In the steady state, the population of galaxies, averaged over large regions, must be the same at all times. Light from distant objects left them long ago, so looking far away is looking into the past. If distant galaxies are systematically different from nearby ones, the Universe has evolved, and the steady-state theory is wrong.
Counting radio sources
After the Second World War, Martin Ryle and his colleagues at Cambridge began surveying the sky with radio telescopes. They catalogued thousands of radio sources, most of them radio galaxies: galaxies ejecting jets of fast-moving particles from their centres, which shine brightly at radio wavelengths.
The test is in the counts. Imagine sources with a fixed luminosity, spread uniformly through a static, unchanging Euclidean space. Sources brighter than flux S lie within a sphere of radius ∝ S^(−1/2). The number of such sources, N(>S), is proportional to the volume, so

N(>S) ∝ S^(−3/2)

Any departure from this law means either that space is not Euclidean or that the sources were different in the past.

Figure 4.1. Radio source counts divided by the static Euclidean expectation (schematic). A non-evolving population would lie on the flat line. The observed counts rise well above it at intermediate fluxes: there are too many faint, distant sources. At the faintest fluxes the counts fall again, because the expansion of the Universe dims and thins out the most distant sources.
Ryle's counts, published through the 1950s and early 1960s, showed too many faint sources. Radio galaxies were more numerous, or more luminous, in the distant past than they are today. Expansion alone, in any model, makes the counts fall below the Euclidean line, not above it. So the excess of faint sources is a sign of evolution, and evolution contradicts the basic principle of the steady-state theory.
Quasars
In 1963 Maarten Schmidt identified the radio source 3C 273 with a star-like object whose spectrum showed the hydrogen lines of a galaxy redshifted by z = 0.158. At the distance implied by Hubble's law it is hundreds of times more luminous than an entire galaxy like the Milky Way. These quasars ("quasi-stellar radio sources") are now known to be powered by gas falling into supermassive black holes at the centres of galaxies.
Quasars give the same verdict as radio galaxies, and more clearly. They are rare nearby and far more common at high redshift, with their numbers peaking at z ≈ 2, about 10 billion years ago. The Universe of the past contained objects that hardly exist today. The Universe evolves.
The steady-state theory was not given up immediately; the counts could be argued about. The decisive blow came in 1965, with the discovery described in Chapter 7.

chapters/ch05-olbers-paradox.html.title: Chapter 5: Olbers' Paradox and Its Resolution
chapters/ch05-olbers-paradox.html.body:
Chapter 5: Olbers' Paradox and Its Resolution
Why is the sky dark at night?
The question sounds childish, but it has a long history. It was raised by Kepler in 1610 and by Edmond Halley and Jean-Philippe de Chéseaux in the 18th century, and is named after Heinrich Olbers, who discussed it in 1823. Its answer turns out to say something deep about the Universe.
The paradox
Suppose the Universe is infinite in extent, unchanging and infinitely old, and filled uniformly with stars. Divide space into thin concentric shells centred on the Earth.

The number of stars in a shell of radius r grows in proportion to its area, ∝ r².
The light we receive from each of those stars falls off as 1/r².

The two effects cancel exactly: every shell contributes the same amount of light. With infinitely many shells, the total would be infinite. In fact nearer stars block the light of more distant ones behind them, so the true conclusion is that every line of sight eventually ends on the surface of a star. The whole sky should blaze as brightly as the surface of an average star, like the Sun's disk spread from horizon to horizon.
It is like standing in a large forest: in whatever direction you look, your line of sight eventually meets a tree trunk.

Figure 5.1. (a) In an infinite, static, eternal universe, the number of stars in each shell (∝ r²) exactly compensates for their faintness (∝ 1/r²), and every line of sight ends on a star. (b) If the Universe has a finite age, we can only see stars within the distance light has travelled since they formed. Light from beyond this horizon has not yet reached us.
The resolution
As E. R. Harrison emphasised, conventional cosmology gives two independent ways out:

(a) The expansion of the Universe. The cosmological redshift reduces the energy of each photon from a distant star, and stretches out the rate at which photons arrive. Distant stars therefore contribute less than the simple Euclidean argument assumes.
(b) A finite age. If the stars have shone for only a finite time, light from stars beyond a certain distance has simply not had time to reach us, whatever the expansion is doing.

Harrison's calculations showed that (b) is by far the more important. Expansion reduces the brightness of the night sky only by a factor of about two compared with a static universe of the same age. The sky is dark mainly because the Universe, and the stars in it, have not existed long enough to fill space with light. Even within our horizon, there are far too few stars, shining for far too short a time, to cover the sky. Stars burn for billions of years, but the time it would take for their light to fill the Universe is around 10²³ years.
(A finite age as the answer was first suggested, remarkably, by the writer Edgar Allan Poe, in his prose poem Eureka of 1848.)
Why this matters for the Big Bang
In the steady-state theory, the Universe is infinitely old, so only the expansion argument is available. (It does work there, because a steady-state universe has been expanding forever, and that limits how much light distant sources can contribute.) In the Big Bang theory, expansion and a finite age go hand in hand. The dark night sky, the most ordinary observation of all, is evidence that the Universe has a history.

chapters/ch06-prediction-cosmic-backgrou.title: Chapter 6: The Prediction of Cosmic Background Radiation
chapters/ch06-prediction-cosmic-backgrou.body:
Chapter 6: The Prediction of Cosmic Background Radiation
Gamow's hot Big Bang
In the late 1940s George Gamow, with his students Ralph Alpher and Robert Herman, asked where the chemical elements came from. Their idea was that the elements were built up by nuclear reactions in the first minutes after the Big Bang, when the whole Universe was as hot as the core of a star.
For nuclear reactions to proceed fast enough, before the rapid expansion of the early Universe thinned the matter out, the Universe must have started at an extremely high temperature. Matter that hot would be filled with thermal radiation, and in the early Universe the energy density of this radiation would greatly exceed that of the matter.
Gamow's hope that all the elements were made this way turned out to be wrong. There is no stable nucleus with mass 5 or mass 8, so the build-up of heavier nuclei by adding one particle at a time stalls at helium, apart from a trace of lithium. The heavier elements were made much later, inside stars and stellar explosions (Burbidge, Burbidge, Fowler and Hoyle, 1957). But the hot early Universe was right, and so was its most important consequence.
A relic radiation
As the Universe expanded, both matter and radiation cooled. After a time the matter became too cool and too thin for further nuclear reactions. Later still (we now know it was about 380 000 years after the beginning), the temperature fell to about 3 000 K. At that point electrons and nuclei combined into neutral atoms, and the Universe became transparent. From then on the radiation was no longer in contact with matter and simply travelled freely through space.
As the Universe continued to expand, each photon was redshifted. It can be shown that radiation which starts with a thermal (blackbody) spectrum keeps a perfect blackbody spectrum as it is redshifted, but with a temperature that falls in proportion to the expansion:

T ∝ 1/a, i.e. T(today) = T(then) / (1 + z)

So the Universe today should be filled with blackbody radiation at a temperature only a few degrees above absolute zero. At such temperatures the radiation is at microwave wavelengths.

Figure 6.1. From prediction to discovery. The background was predicted in 1948 but not searched for until the mid-1960s, when it was found by accident.
Predictions, forgotten and remade
In 1948 Alpher and Herman estimated that the present temperature of this radiation should be about 5 K. Gamow's own estimates over the following years varied, some reaching tens of kelvin. No-one at the time took up the challenge of looking for the radiation. Many radio astronomers did not know of the prediction, and those who did assumed it was too faint to detect against other sources of noise. The prediction was largely forgotten.
In the early 1960s it was rediscovered independently. At Princeton, Robert Dicke and Jim Peebles were reconsidering the hot Big Bang. One of their reasons was that stars did not seem able to produce the observed abundance of helium (Chapter 9). Peebles calculated that the present radiation temperature should be a few kelvin. Dicke, with Peter Roll and David Wilkinson, set out to build a radiometer to detect it. They were beaten to the discovery, as the next chapter tells, by a few months and by about 50 km.
(Peebles received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019 for his theoretical work in cosmology.)

chapters/ch07-discovery-cmb.html.title: Chapter 7: The Discovery of Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation
chapters/ch07-discovery-cmb.html.body:
Chapter 7: The Discovery of the Cosmic Microwave Background
An unexplained hiss
In 1964 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, two radio astronomers at Bell Telephone Laboratories in Holmdel, New Jersey, were preparing a 6-metre horn antenna for radio astronomy. The antenna had originally been built for early satellite communication experiments. They intended to use it for precise measurements of radio emission from our Galaxy, so they first needed to account for every source of noise in their equipment.
Working at a wavelength of 7.35 cm (4.08 GHz), they found a small excess of noise, equivalent to a temperature of about 3.5 K, that would not go away. It was the same in every direction, at every time of day and in every season. They checked the electronics and pointed the antenna away from cities. They even evicted a pair of pigeons nesting in the horn and cleaned out what they politely called "white dielectric material". The excess remained.
The connection is made
Penzias mentioned the puzzle to Bernard Burke of MIT. Burke had heard about a talk by Jim Peebles predicting a background of radiation at a few kelvin, and put the two groups in touch. Dicke's group, only about 50 km away in Princeton, came to Holmdel, saw the data, and recognised that they had been scooped.
In 1965 the two groups published companion papers in the Astrophysical Journal: Penzias and Wilson reporting "excess antenna temperature" at 4 080 Mc/s, and Dicke, Peebles, Roll and Wilkinson explaining it as cosmic blackbody radiation left over from the hot Big Bang.
The cosmic microwave background (CMB) was exactly what the hot Big Bang theory had predicted. The steady-state theory had no natural way to produce it, a uniform blackbody glow filling all of space. Its discovery was the decisive blow to the steady-state theory. Penzias and Wilson were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1978.
A perfect blackbody
One measurement at one wavelength does not show that the radiation is a blackbody. That required measurements across the spectrum, especially at millimetre wavelengths near the peak, which are absorbed by the atmosphere. Through the 1970s and 1980s measurements from mountains, balloons and rockets gave temperatures of roughly 2.7–3 K, but with confusing discrepancies.
The question was settled by NASA's Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) satellite. In 1990, after just nine minutes of observation, its FIRAS instrument showed a spectrum that matched a blackbody so perfectly that the data points lay on the theoretical curve. The audience at the American Astronomical Society meeting gave the slide a standing ovation. The final analysis gives

T = 2.7255 ± 0.0006 K

and limits any departure from a pure blackbody to less than 50 parts per million. It is the most perfect blackbody spectrum ever measured in nature.

Figure 7.1. The spectrum of the cosmic microwave background. The curve is a blackbody at 2.7255 K, peaking at about 160 GHz (a wavelength of about 2 mm). The points mark the frequencies measured by COBE's FIRAS instrument; the real error bars are far too small to see, so here they are drawn 400 times larger. The diamond marks the single wavelength of Penzias and Wilson's discovery, far down on the long-wavelength side of the peak.
Ripples
The CMB is almost, but not quite, the same in every direction. COBE's DMR instrument found in 1992 that its temperature varies from place to place by about 1 part in 100 000. These tiny ripples are the imprint of slight variations in density in the early Universe. Gravity later amplified them into the galaxies and clusters of the cosmic web (Chapter 3). John Mather and George Smoot shared the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics for COBE's results. Mapping the ripples in detail has since become one of the most powerful tools in cosmology (Chapter 11).
There are about 410 CMB photons in every cubic centimetre of space. A small fraction of the "snow" on an old analogue television tuned between stations came from the Big Bang.

chapters/ch08-hot-big-bang.html.title: Chapter 8: The Hot Big Bang
chapters/ch08-hot-big-bang.html.body:
Chapter 8: The Hot Big Bang
We now follow the theoretical consequences of the Penzias–Wilson discovery backwards in time.
Radiation in an expanding Universe
The wavelength λ_max at which blackbody radiation is brightest is fixed by its temperature, through Wien's displacement law:

λ_max × T = 2.898 mm·K

As the Universe expands, every wavelength is stretched in proportion to the scale factor a(t) (Chapter 3):

λ_max ∝ a

So the temperature of the radiation must fall as the Universe expands:

T_rad ∝ 1/a

At redshift z, when the Universe was 1 + z times smaller, the radiation was 1 + z times hotter: T = 2.7255 K × (1 + z).
Radiation versus matter
How do the energy densities of radiation and matter change with the expansion? (Energy density is expressed as an equivalent mass density through E = mc².)

Matter. The number of particles is fixed, and their volume grows as a³. So ρ_m ∝ a⁻³.
Radiation. The number of photons per unit volume also falls as a⁻³. In addition, each photon's wavelength is stretched, so its energy falls as a⁻¹. So ρ_rad ∝ a⁻⁴.

The ratio is ρ_rad / ρ_m ∝ 1/a. Radiation becomes relatively more important the further back we go.
Today matter dominates. Counting all the matter (including the dark matter of Chapter 11), and including the neutrinos that accompany the photons, radiation makes up only about 1/3 400 of the energy density of matter. So at a redshift of about 3 400, when the Universe was some 3 400 times smaller than now and about 50 000 years old, the two were equal. Before that the Universe was radiation-dominated.

Figure 8.1. The mass-energy density of radiation, matter and dark energy as the Universe expands, plotted against 1 + z. Going back in time is moving to the right. Radiation (∝ (1 + z)⁴) rises fastest and overtakes matter at 1 + z ≈ 3 400. Dark energy, constant per unit volume, only became dominant in the last few billion years (Chapter 11).
The thermal history
Following the temperature backwards gives the outline of cosmic history.

Figure 8.2. The temperature of the cosmic radiation against time since the Big Bang, calculated for the Planck 2018 cosmology. Note the logarithmic scales: the first three minutes and the last 13.8 billion years appear on the same chart.

Today, 13.8 billion years: 2.7 K. Galaxies, stars, planets.
About 380 000 years: about 3 000 K, at z ≈ 1 100. Electrons and nuclei combine into atoms (recombination); the Universe becomes transparent and the CMB is released. Before this time the Universe was an opaque, glowing plasma, like the inside of a star. The CMB is a picture of the surface where it became transparent.
About 50 000 years: matter and radiation densities equal.
A few minutes: about 10⁹ K. The light nuclei are formed (Chapter 9).
One second: about 10¹⁰ K. Neutrinos stop interacting and stream away freely.
Earlier still: temperatures and densities beyond anything reachable in laboratories, where our knowledge of physics becomes increasingly uncertain.

There are about 1.6 billion photons for every proton or neutron in the Universe. This enormous ratio is fixed by the expansion; it has hardly changed since the first second. It will matter in the next chapter.
What "Big Bang" does and does not mean
The early Universe was hot, dense and dominated by radiation: it was exceedingly bright. From that state it has expanded and cooled ever since, and as galaxies formed they too were carried along by the expansion.
It is tempting to picture this as an explosion: a lump of matter at a point, bursting outwards into empty space. That picture is wrong, and the name "Big Bang" encourages it.

There is no centre. As Figure 3.3 showed, every galaxy sees all the others receding in the same way.
There is no outside. The Big Bang did not happen at a place within space; it happened everywhere. At early times all of space, possibly infinite, was hot and dense, and all of space has been expanding since.
What the theory describes is the expansion of space, starting from a hot, dense state. It does not describe a "moment of creation". As we follow time back towards the very beginning, densities and temperatures increase without limit, and general relativity, which does not include quantum effects, ceases to be reliable. What happened at "t = 0", if anything, is still unknown.

chapters/ch09-big-bang-nucleosynthesis.h.title: Chapter 9: Big Bang Nucleosynthesis
chapters/ch09-big-bang-nucleosynthesis.h.body:
Chapter 9: Big Bang Nucleosynthesis
The helium abundance: a confirmation of the Big Bang theory
About a quarter of the mass of ordinary matter in the Universe is helium. It is found in roughly that proportion everywhere: in old stars and young, in our Galaxy and in distant ones. Stars do make helium by fusing hydrogen, but all the stars that have ever shone could have made only a few per cent. The rest must have been made before there were any stars. This chapter shows that the hot Big Bang predicts almost exactly the amount observed. The calculation is simple enough to do in a few lines.
The first second: neutrons and protons in equilibrium
At temperatures above about 10¹² K (in the first hundredth of a second or so), pairs of particles and antiparticles were continually being created from radiation and annihilating back into it. As the temperature fell, the pairs annihilated. Because of a slight excess of matter over antimatter, about one part in a billion, a small residue of protons and neutrons was left over. Everything made of ordinary matter today comes from this residue.
These protons and neutrons were bathed in an intense sea of electrons, positrons, neutrinos and photons. Weak nuclear reactions continually converted protons into neutrons and back again:

p + e⁻ ⇌ n + ν
p + ν̄ ⇌ n + e⁺

While these reactions are fast, the neutrons and protons are in thermal equilibrium. The neutron is slightly heavier than the proton (Δm c² = (m_n − m_p)c² = 1.293 MeV), so making a neutron costs energy, and their relative numbers follow the Boltzmann law:

n / p = exp[ −(m_n − m_p) c² / kT ]

At T = 10¹⁰ K, kT = 0.86 MeV, and the formula gives n/p = e^(−1.5) ≈ 0.22, about one neutron for every five protons. As the temperature continues to fall, the equilibrium ratio would keep falling towards zero.
Freeze-out
But the weak reactions depend steeply on temperature. When the Universe is about a second old (kT ≈ 0.8 MeV), they become too slow to keep up with the expansion; the neutrinos effectively stop interacting. The conversion of protons into neutrons stops and the ratio freezes at n/p ≈ 1/5.
From then on, the only process changing the number of neutrons is their own radioactive decay:

n → p + e⁻ + ν̄   (mean lifetime 879 s, nearly 15 minutes)


Figure 9.1. A simplified history of the neutron-to-proton ratio. At first it follows thermal equilibrium (dashed line). It freezes out at about 1/5 when the weak reactions stop, then slowly falls as free neutrons decay, until they are locked safely into nuclei at about 200 seconds.
The deuterium bottleneck
The first step towards helium is the formation of deuterium (heavy hydrogen):

n + p → ²H + γ

The deuteron is fragile: its binding energy is only 2.2 MeV. Even when the typical photon energy is far below this, there are 1.6 billion photons for every nucleon (Chapter 8). The rare photons in the high-energy tail of the blackbody spectrum are still numerous enough to break up every deuteron as soon as it forms. Deuterium can survive only when the temperature has fallen below about 10⁹ K, at an age of about 3 minutes (≈ 200 s).
During this delay neutrons continue to decay, and n/p falls from about 1/5 to about 1/7. (The simplified model of Figure 9.1, with an abrupt freeze-out, gives 1/6.5. In the full calculation freeze-out is gradual, and the ratio ends close to 1/7.)
Making helium
Once deuterium survives, a rapid chain of reactions converts almost all of it into helium-4, the most tightly bound light nucleus:

Figure 9.2. The main reactions of Big Bang nucleosynthesis. Almost every neutron ends up in helium-4. The absence of stable nuclei with mass 5 or 8 blocks the path to heavier elements, leaving only a trace of lithium-7.
Each helium-4 nucleus contains 2 neutrons and 2 protons, and essentially every surviving neutron ends up in one. So the fraction of the mass that becomes helium, Y, is simply:

Y = (mass in helium) / (total mass) = 2 (n/p) / (1 + n/p)

Check with a concrete count. With n/p = 1/7, take 2 neutrons and 14 protons. The 2 neutrons combine with 2 of the protons to make one helium-4 nucleus, of mass 4. The remaining 12 protons are hydrogen. The total mass is 16, so

Y = 4/16 = 25%

Had we ignored neutron decay and used n/p = 1/5, we would have obtained 2 neutrons + 10 protons → Y = 4/12 ≈ 33%. That is too high: the decay of neutrons during the deuterium bottleneck is exactly what brings the answer down to 25%.
A full computer calculation, following every reaction rate and using the measured density of ordinary matter, gives Y = 0.247.
Comparison with observation
To measure the primordial helium abundance, astronomers look at the least-processed gas they can find: clouds of ionised gas in small galaxies that have formed very few stars and contain very few heavy elements. The result is Y = 0.245 ± 0.003, in remarkable agreement with the prediction.
The Big Bang also leaves traces of other light nuclei, whose abundances depend on how dense ordinary matter was:



Nucleus
Predicted (relative to hydrogen)
Observed




⁴He (mass fraction Y)
0.247
0.245 ± 0.003


Deuterium, D/H
2.5 × 10⁻⁵
(2.53 ± 0.03) × 10⁻⁵


³He/H
~1 × 10⁻⁵
~1 × 10⁻⁵


⁷Li/H
~5 × 10⁻¹⁰
~1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰



Deuterium is a particularly sensitive "baryometer". Stars only destroy it, so any deuterium we see today was made in the Big Bang, and the amount made falls steeply as the matter density rises. The measured D/H fixes the density of ordinary matter at about 5% of the critical density, independently of any other method. This agrees with the value deduced from the CMB ripples (Chapter 11). It is also far less than the total amount of matter, which is strong evidence that most matter is not made of protons and neutrons at all.
Lithium-7 is the exception: the observed abundance in old stars is about three times lower than predicted. Whether this "lithium problem" points to new physics or, more probably, to lithium being destroyed in the stars themselves is still being investigated.
Agreement between theory and observation across nine orders of magnitude in abundance, from helium at 25% to lithium at a part in ten billion, is one of the great successes of the Big Bang theory. Together with the expansion (Chapter 3), the evolution of the Universe (Chapter 4) and the cosmic microwave background (Chapter 7), it forms the observational foundation of modern cosmology.

chapters/ch10-conclusion.html.title: Chapter 10: Conclusion
chapters/ch10-conclusion.html.body:
Chapter 10: Conclusion
We can only imagine between the extremes of the tiniest and the vast. But the timescales and distances we come across in our scientific search are either too tiny or too vast to imagine directly. A proton is 10⁻¹⁵ m across; the observable Universe is 10²⁶ m. Nucleosynthesis was over in minutes; the Universe is 13.8 billion years old. Yet the truth ingrained in the heart of the atom is the same truth embedded in the stars. The helium in the Sun was made by the same nuclear physics that we test in laboratories, in the first three minutes of cosmic history.
The story in this book is a story of a ladder. Parallax gave distances to the nearest stars. The H-R diagram and star clusters extended them across the Galaxy. Cepheids carried the measurement to other galaxies, and there Hubble found the expansion. From the expansion came the idea of a beginning. From the beginning came three predictions: the Universe should evolve, it should be filled with cool blackbody radiation, and it should be one-quarter helium. All three have been confirmed.
It has been only about 10 000 years since the first farmers began to settle. At the end of the 19th century some physicists were confident that the great work of physics was almost finished, and that only the details remained to be filled in. Within a few decades relativity and quantum mechanics had overturned that view, and the expanding Universe had been discovered. In the same way, cosmology has repeatedly found mysteries where it expected answers. In 1998 these were the "missing mass" and the large-scale structure of the Universe. Since then they have been joined by the discovery that the expansion is accelerating, driven by a dark energy that no current theory explains (Chapter 11).
The more we learn, the more we find there is to learn. It may be a very long time before questions like "What is matter?", "What is light?" and "What is gravity?" are answered in their full sense. To those people of the future we may seem like the first farmers of science, just beginning to settle near the banks of the starry, eternal rivers of truth.

chapters/ch11-since-1998.html.title: Chapter 11: The Universe Since 1998
chapters/ch11-since-1998.html.body:
Chapter 11: The Universe Since 1998
The first edition of this book was written in 1998. That year, cosmology changed. This chapter describes what has been learned since. The broad picture of Chapters 1–10 has survived intact, but it has been measured with a precision that would have seemed impossible then, and it has acquired some deep new puzzles.

Figure 11.1. Cosmic history on a logarithmic time scale, as it is understood today.
11.1 The accelerating Universe
In 1998 everyone expected the expansion of the Universe to be slowing down, because the gravity of everything in it pulls everything else back. The open question was by how much. Two teams set out to measure the slowing using Type Ia supernovae: exploding white dwarf stars that, once a correction is made for the shape of their light curves, all reach nearly the same peak luminosity. They are standard candles bright enough to be seen across billions of light-years, and they extend the distance ladder of Chapter 2 by another rung.
If the expansion had been slowing, distant galaxies would have been receding faster in the past, and supernovae at a given redshift would be relatively close and bright. Both the High-z Supernova Search Team (Adam Riess, Brian Schmidt and colleagues) and the Supernova Cosmology Project (Saul Perlmutter and colleagues) found the opposite. The distant supernovae were fainter, so farther away, than expected. The expansion is speeding up.

Figure 11.2. How the brightness of a standard candle depends on redshift in different universes, relative to an empty, coasting universe. In a matter-only universe (orange) the expansion decelerates and distant supernovae appear brighter. The observations follow the blue curve: a universe whose expansion began to accelerate about 6 billion years ago.
Something with a strange property is needed to drive the acceleration: its density stays nearly constant as space expands, and its gravitational effect is repulsive. It has been named dark energy. The simplest candidate is Einstein's cosmological constant, Λ, which he introduced in 1917 and later abandoned: an energy belonging to empty space itself. Perlmutter, Schmidt and Riess shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Why the vacuum should have this energy, and why it is so small (quantum theory naively predicts a value 10¹²⁰ times too large), is perhaps the deepest unsolved problem in physics.
11.2 Precision cosmology from the CMB ripples
The temperature ripples in the cosmic microwave background, first detected by COBE in 1992 (Chapter 7), have since been mapped in great detail: by balloon experiments in the late 1990s, by NASA's WMAP satellite (2001–2010), by ESA's Planck satellite (2009–2013), and by ground-based telescopes in Chile and at the South Pole.
The ripples are the imprint of sound waves that travelled through the hot plasma of the early Universe before it became transparent at 380 000 years. The characteristic size of the ripples on the sky is a ruler of known length at a known distance. It shows that space is geometrically flat to within less than 1%. The detailed pattern fixes the contents of the Universe precisely. The same sound waves left a faint preferred separation of about 150 Mpc between galaxies, the baryon acoustic oscillation scale, which was found in galaxy surveys in 2005 and has become another standard ruler.
From Planck and these other measurements:



Quantity
Value




Age of the Universe
13.787 ± 0.020 billion years


Hubble constant (inferred)
67.4 ± 0.5 km/s/Mpc


CMB temperature
2.7255 K


Geometry
flat




Figure 11.3. The contents of the Universe today, by energy density. Everything ever seen through a telescope, all the stars, gas, planets and people, is in the small aqua slice.
11.3 Dark matter
The "missing mass" mentioned in the 1998 conclusion has a long history. Fritz Zwicky found in 1933 that the galaxies in the Coma cluster move too fast to be held together by the visible matter. In the 1970s Vera Rubin and others found the same in the rotation of individual spiral galaxies.
The evidence is now overwhelming and comes from many independent directions: the CMB ripples, the bending of light by clusters of galaxies (gravitational lensing), the growth of the cosmic web, and colliding galaxy clusters such as the Bullet Cluster, where the mass is clearly separated from the visible gas. Combined with the nucleosynthesis limit on ordinary matter (Chapter 9), this shows that about 85% of the matter in the Universe is not made of atoms. It does not emit or absorb light and interacts, as far as we know, only through gravity. What it is remains unknown. Decades of increasingly sensitive laboratory searches have not yet detected a dark-matter particle.
11.4 The Hubble tension
The distance ladder of Chapter 2 has been rebuilt with modern tools: Gaia parallaxes, Hubble Space Telescope (and now JWST) observations of Cepheids, and Type Ia supernovae. It gives H₀ ≈ 73 km/s/Mpc. Planck's measurement of the early Universe, extrapolated to today using the standard model, gives 67.4 km/s/Mpc. The uncertainties are now so small that the difference is significant at about the 5σ level.

Figure 11.4. A selection of measurements of the Hubble constant. The early-Universe prediction (blue) and the Cepheid–supernova distance ladder (orange) disagree; other methods fall in between or are not yet precise enough to decide.
Either some systematic error is hiding in one of the measurements, or the standard cosmological model is missing something. This question, about the same constant Hubble first measured in 1929, is one of the most active in cosmology today.
11.5 Is dark energy changing?
If dark energy is Einstein's cosmological constant, its density never changes. Recent results from the DESI galaxy survey, combined with the CMB and supernovae, have hinted that dark energy may instead be slowly weakening with time. The evidence is not yet decisive. If confirmed, it would mean that dark energy is not a constant of nature, but something dynamic.
11.6 New windows

Gaia (launched 2013) has measured parallaxes and motions for over a billion stars of our Galaxy, putting the bottom rung of the distance ladder on a new footing.
Gravitational waves, ripples in space-time itself, were detected by LIGO in 2015 from a pair of merging black holes (Nobel Prize 2017). In 2017 a merger of two neutron stars was seen both in gravitational waves and in light. The gravitational waves gave its distance directly, without any distance ladder, and the light gave its redshift, providing a completely independent measurement of H₀ (Figure 11.4). Such "standard sirens" may one day help resolve the Hubble tension.
The James Webb Space Telescope (launched 2021) observes in the infrared, where the light of the most distant galaxies has been redshifted. It has found galaxies at redshifts beyond 14, seen less than 300 million years after the Big Bang. Many are more luminous and more mature than expected, and astronomers are still working out why.

11.7 Before the hot Big Bang: inflation
The hot Big Bang leaves some questions unanswered. Why is space so flat? Why is the CMB the same temperature in regions that, according to the simple theory, could never have been in contact? Where did the tiny ripples come from?
The theory of inflation, proposed by Alan Guth in 1980 and developed by Andrei Linde, Andreas Albrecht and Paul Steinhardt, among others, suggests that in a tiny fraction of a second before the hot Big Bang, space expanded exponentially by an enormous factor. This would have flattened space, smoothed it out, and stretched microscopic quantum fluctuations into the seeds of galaxies. The detailed statistics of the CMB ripples match inflation's predictions well. Its most distinctive signature, a pattern in the polarisation of the CMB produced by primordial gravitational waves, has not yet been detected. (A claimed detection in 2014 turned out to be caused by dust in our own Galaxy.)
11.8 The picture today
The standard model of cosmology, called ΛCDM (Lambda, for dark energy, plus Cold Dark Matter), describes an enormous range of observations with just six numbers. It is the hot Big Bang of this book, made precise. Yet 95% of its content, dark matter and dark energy, is of unknown nature. In 1998 the conclusion of this book said: "the more we learn, the more we find there is to learn." Nearly three decades of discovery have proved it right.

chapters/changes.html.title: Changes from the First Edition
chapters/changes.html.body:
Changes from the First Edition
The first edition (1998) is preserved unchanged. This page lists what this edition changes, so that the two can be compared.
Corrections of fact



Chapter
First edition
Second edition




2
Cepheid luminosity is "directly proportional" to period, L ∝ P
Luminosity grows as a power of the period; the Leavitt law is linear in log P: M_V = −2.43 (log P − 1) − 4.05


2
Moving-cluster method described only as a change in angular size
Explained with the convergent point and the formula d = v_r tan θ / (4.74 μ); the angular-size picture kept as an equivalent view


2
Parallax works "up to 300 light years"
True for ground-based work in 1998; Gaia now reaches thousands of parsecs


3
Distant galaxies "receding fastest at 1200 km/s"
Hubble's 1929 sample reached about 1 000 km/s; by 1931 Humason had measured nearly 20 000 km/s


3
Humason, 1933, cluster in Ursa Major
Date and object could not be confirmed; replaced with the documented Hubble & Humason (1931) result


3
Credit for the expansion to Hubble alone
Slipher's redshifts and Lemaître's 1927 derivation acknowledged; IAU's 2018 name "Hubble–Lemaître law" noted


6
Gamow proposed that "many of the heavy elements" were made in the Big Bang
Correct as history, but the idea failed: no stable mass-5 or mass-8 nuclei, so only light elements are made; heavy elements come from stars


6
Prediction attributed to Gamow only
Alpher & Herman's 1948 prediction of ≈ 5 K added


7
"Dickie"
Dicke


7
"Excess noise in their sources"
Excess noise in their antenna


7
"The discovery … was a direct prediction of the Big Bang theory"
The CMB was a prediction; its discovery confirmed it


7

2.7255 K (COBE FIRAS)


8
Matter–radiation equality at z ≈ 10³
z ≈ 3 400 once dark matter and neutrinos are included


8
The primordial state "exploded in a big bang"
The Big Bang was the expansion of space everywhere, not an explosion from a point into space


9
"More sophisticated analysis yields 25%"
The step is explained: neutron decay during the deuterium bottleneck lowers n/p from 1/5 to 1/7, giving Y = 25%


9
Stars begin with 20–30% helium
Primordial helium now measured as Y = 0.245 ± 0.003


References
Lonely Heart of the Cosmos
Lonely Hearts of the Cosmos (Overbye's title); publishers and years added


10
"In the beginning of the 19th century, scientists were confident that by the end of the century…"
The well-known overconfidence was at the end of the 19th century



Figures

All scanned figures from published textbooks have been removed. Besides avoiding copyright problems, several of them illustrated a different topic from the text around them (galaxy photographs in the nucleosynthesis chapter; star-cluster photographs in the hot Big Bang chapter). Some image files combined two unrelated figures.
26 new diagrams were drawn from physical formulae or published, cited values. They are generated by scripts/make_figures.py.
Figure numbering is now consistent within each chapter (Figure 2.1, 2.2, …). The first edition mixed its own numbering with the source textbooks' numbering.
Where a figure uses illustrative rather than real data points, its caption says so.

Additions

Chapter 1: the light-gathering and resolution formulae; detectors; spectroscopy; radio and space astronomy.
Chapter 2: the distance ladder; the distance modulus; the parsec; Leavitt's discovery; Baade's 1952 revision.
Chapter 3: the definition of redshift; what uniform expansion means; a numerical value for the Hubble time; how the true age differs from 1/H₀; modern redshift surveys.
Chapter 4: the steady-state theory explained; why source counts test it; quasars.
Chapter 5: the history of the paradox and why finite age is the main resolution.
Chapter 7: COBE and the precise blackbody spectrum; the CMB anisotropies.
Chapter 8: the thermal history of the Universe; what the Big Bang does and does not mean.
Chapter 9: freeze-out, the deuterium bottleneck, the other light elements, and the lithium problem.
Chapter 11 (new): the accelerating Universe, precision cosmology, dark matter, the Hubble tension, new observational windows and inflation.

Style

Gendered language ("man", "men of the future") replaced with neutral equivalents. The meaning and the closing image of the conclusion are kept.
Equations are written consistently in Unicode, with symbols defined where they are first used.

chapters/references.html.body:
References and Further Reading
Sources of the first edition

Frank H. Shu, The Physical Universe: An Introduction to Astronomy. University Science Books, 1982.
Robert C. Smith, Observational Astrophysics. Cambridge University Press, 1995.
Robert Wagoner and Donald Goldsmith, Cosmic Horizons: Understanding the Universe. W. H. Freeman, 1983.
Dennis Overbye, Lonely Hearts of the Cosmos. HarperCollins, 1991.
Charles R. Cowley, An Introduction to Cosmochemistry. Cambridge University Press, 1995.
Ian D. Lawrie, A Unified Grand Tour of Theoretical Physics. Adam Hilger, 1990.

Further reading

Barbara Ryden, Introduction to Cosmology, 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press, 2016. A clear undergraduate text covering everything in this book with full derivations.
Edward R. Harrison, Darkness at Night: A Riddle of the Universe. Harvard University Press, 1987. The history and resolution of Olbers' paradox.
Steven Weinberg, The First Three Minutes, updated ed. Basic Books, 1993. The classic popular account of the hot Big Bang and nucleosynthesis.
P. J. E. Peebles, Cosmology's Century. Princeton University Press, 2020. A history of modern cosmology by one of its makers.

Key papers cited in this edition

H. S. Leavitt and E. C. Pickering, "Periods of 25 Variable Stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud", Harvard College Observatory Circular 173 (1912).
E. Hubble, "A Relation between Distance and Radial Velocity among Extra-Galactic Nebulae", PNAS 15, 168 (1929).
R. A. Alpher and R. Herman, "Evolution of the Universe", Nature 162, 774 (1948).
A. A. Penzias and R. W. Wilson, "A Measurement of Excess Antenna Temperature at 4080 Mc/s", ApJ 142, 419 (1965).
R. H. Dicke, P. J. E. Peebles, P. G. Roll and D. T. Wilkinson, "Cosmic Black-Body Radiation", ApJ 142, 414 (1965).
A. G. Riess et al., "Observational Evidence from Supernovae for an Accelerating Universe and a Cosmological Constant", AJ 116, 1009 (1998).
S. Perlmutter et al., "Measurements of Ω and Λ from 42 High-Redshift Supernovae", ApJ 517, 565 (1999).
G. F. Benedict et al., "Hubble Space Telescope Fine Guidance Sensor Parallaxes of Galactic Cepheid Variable Stars: Period-Luminosity Relations", AJ 133, 1810 (2007). (The period–luminosity relation of Figure 2.8.)
D. J. Fixsen, "The Temperature of the Cosmic Microwave Background", ApJ 707, 916 (2009).
Planck Collaboration, "Planck 2018 results. VI. Cosmological parameters", A&A 641, A6 (2020).
R. J. Cooke, M. Pettini and C. C. Steidel, "One Percent Determination of the Primordial Deuterium Abundance", ApJ 855, 102 (2018).
E. Aver et al., "Improving helium abundance determinations with Leo P as a case study", JCAP 03, 027 (2021).
A. G. Riess et al., "A Comprehensive Measurement of the Local Value of the Hubble Constant with 1 km/s/Mpc Uncertainty from the Hubble Space Telescope and the SH0ES Team", ApJL 934, L7 (2022).
W. L. Freedman, "Measurements of the Hubble Constant: Tensions in Perspective", ApJ 919, 16 (2021).
K. C. Wong et al., "H0LiCOW XIII", MNRAS 498, 1420 (2020).
B. P. Abbott et al., "A gravitational-wave standard siren measurement of the Hubble constant", Nature 551, 85 (2017).
